case_study_insert.main_stem: Meridian Learning Centre (MLC) is a private limited company in the education sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2014 by Priya Raman, it delivers exam-preparation courses to school pupils across the region and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. MLC plans to invest $360,000 in a new e-learning recording studio, financed by a $200,000 share issue and $160,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $20 a unit and a selling price of $65, and delivers 11,000 units of tuition a year. MLC faces two problems: tutor absenteeism has reached 10% and complaints about misprinted workbooks are rising, threatening its 96% pass rate.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — 2025: A survey of 800 parents found that 72% wanted weekend classes and 61% would pay $12 more for recorded lessons; average satisfaction was 4.3 out of 5. The centre logged 45 workbook complaints last term, up from 31, and printed 9,800 workbooks at a waste rate of 3%. Tutor marking took an average of 4.2 days. A local college offers a $580 certificate course in e-learning production.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Meridian Learning Centre for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.9% to 4.4%, increasing the cost of business borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.8% to $13.60 an hour from April 2026, raising wage costs for tutors and support staff. (3) Printing and paper input costs have risen 8.6% year-on-year, while household spending on private tutoring grew 3.1% and exam-board licence fees rose 5.5%.

questions.question_text: MLC plans to fund its new recording studio with a $200,000 share issue rather than using its $160,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for MLC of the share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $200,000 share issue raises more money than the $160,000 of retained profit and does not drain the cash balance MLC needs to cover fixed costs of $270,000 a year and the 10% tutor absenteeism disruption. New share capital gives Priya Raman the full $360,000 studio without sacrificing working capital, so the $160,000 retained profit stays available as a cushion if recorded lessons take longer than expected to attract the 61% of parents willing to pay $12 more.

Point 2: Share capital does not have to be repaid and requires no interest, unlike a loan, so it places no strain on the operating profit that supports MLC's 96% pass rate and its rising workbook-quality costs. Issuing shares to outside investors may also bring useful contacts or e-learning expertise, and because MLC is a private limited company it can pass them the risk of the $360,000 studio while keeping day-to-day control in the hierarchical structure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to MLC's funding choice, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: MLC wants to fill places on its new recorded lesson courses. Consider local newspaper advertising, partnerships with schools, or paid social media advertising. Which should MLC choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: A newspaper campaign can reach parents across the region cheaply and suits a message about weekend classes near their children's schools. It is far less expensive than the $360,000 studio investment, so it will not strain the $270,000 fixed-cost base. However, readership is ageing and untargeted, so many readers have no school-age children, and a static advert cannot demonstrate recorded lessons or capture the 61% of the 800 surveyed parents who would pay $12 more.

Partnerships with schools: Agreeing referral links with local schools would put MLC's exam-preparation courses directly in front of pupils and parents at virtually no media cost, supporting the 96% pass rate reputation and generating steady weekend-class enrolments. The weakness is speed: school approvals are slow, schools may favour rival providers, and the partnerships alone may not fill enough places quickly to cover the new studio's costs.

Paid social media advertising: Targeted ads can reach parents of exam-age pupils by interest and location, can show short clips from the recorded lessons, and can be measured and adjusted daily. This speaks directly to the 72% of surveyed parents wanting weekend classes and the 61% willing to pay $12 more, and can drive sign-ups while the studio is new. Costs can escalate if campaigns are poorly managed, and pupils without social-media-using parents could be missed.

Recommendation: MLC should choose paid social media advertising. It targets the exact parents identified in the 800-person survey, demonstrates the recorded lessons that justify the $360,000 spend, and can be controlled to protect cash. Newspaper advertising is rejected as untargeted and wasteful; school partnerships are rejected as too slow to fill places immediately, though they should be pursued later as a low-cost supplement.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the promotional options with little application to MLC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MLC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MLC with a well-justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

questions.question_text: MLC's tutor absenteeism has reached 10%. Explain two benefits for MLC of using autocratic leadership to tackle this problem.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Priya Raman set clear, firm attendance rules and a single strict timetable for the 30 staff, which suits the hierarchical structure and can quickly cut the 10% absenteeism that is disrupting 11,000 units of tuition. Quick decisions on cover and punctuality are valuable when 45 workbook complaints have already risen and the 96% pass rate is at risk.

Point 2: A directive leader can reallocate marking and teaching duties without lengthy consultation, keeping the 9,800 workbooks and exam courses on schedule despite absences. This decisiveness supports the launch of the $360,000 e-learning studio, because a top-down instruction to adopt the new recorded lessons can be enforced fast, and the $580 college course can be mandated for the tutors who need production skills, protecting output while the studio beds in. Clear top-down instructions also help tutors accept the new recorded-lesson routines demanded by 61% of the 800 surveyed parents, so absence does not undermine the $360,000 investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MLC's absenteeism, complaints and studio launch.

questions.question_text: MLC must cut the 3% waste rate on misprinted workbooks. Consider in-house inspection of every batch or a quality assurance agreement with the printer. Which should MLC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
In-house inspection: Checking each batch before it reaches tutors catches misprints directly and protects the 96% pass rate and the 45 workbook complaints that have risen from 31. Quality control by inspection is under MLC's own control and needs no supplier cooperation, which suits Priya Raman's autocratic style. It is labour-intensive, however: with a workforce of 30 already suffering 10% absenteeism, assigning staff to check 9,800 workbooks diverts them from teaching, and inspection detects errors only after printing, so the 3% waste has already been incurred.

Quality assurance agreement: Working with the printer to prevent errors at source — agreed paper standards, proof approvals and process checks — attacks the 3% waste rate before it happens, cutting the cost of reprints and the 45 complaints. It is cheaper in staff time and can be written into the supply contract for the $360,000 studio's workbooks. The limits are that MLC must trust and monitor the supplier, agreed standards may raise the unit price, and a weak printer could still fail, leaving MLC exposed during the studio launch.

Decision: MLC should choose the quality assurance agreement with the printer. Prevention removes the cause of the 3% waste and the complaint rise without pulling tutors off 11,000 units of tuition, and it fits the limited 30-person workforce. In-house inspection is rejected because it is slow, ties up absentee-prone staff and only finds faults after the paper is wasted; a small final spot-check can be retained as a cheap safety net, especially while 4.2-day marking times leave little slack.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two quality approaches with limited application to MLC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of MLC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of MLC with a well-justified decision covering cost, staffing and prevention.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MLC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($65 − $20) = $270,000 ÷ $45 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units of tuition a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $65 − $20 = $45. Answer: contribution per unit is $45.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MLC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with 11,000 units of tuition delivered to find a margin of safety of 5,000 units, showing how many course places could be lost before MLC stops covering its $270,000 fixed costs while the studio launches.
2. Use the $45 contribution per unit to test pricing: a $12 premium for recorded lessons would lift contribution to $57, helping justify the $360,000 studio, whereas a $5 discount would cut it to $40 and require more places.
3. Use fixed costs and contribution to set the enrolment target needed to justify the $200,000 share issue and the $160,000 retained profit invested, so Priya Raman can judge whether the studio earns its cost.
4. Use average total cost ($270,000 ÷ 11,000 units + $20 = $24.55 + $20 = $44.55 a unit) and labour productivity (11,000 units ÷ 30 staff = 366.67 units per worker) to benchmark the studio's first year, monitor the 10% absenteeism drag and control the 8.6% paper-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $45 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 5,000 units; pricing the $12 premium using $45 contribution; enrolment target for the $200,000 share issue; and unit cost $44.55 with productivity 366.67 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MLC's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has MLC's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 50.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 a gross profit of $720,000 on revenue of $1,600,000 gives 45.0%; in 2025 $1,000,000 on $2,000,000 gives 50.0%. Operating profit of $200,000 against $1,600,000 revenue gives 12.5% in 2024, and $300,000 against $2,000,000 gives 15.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $200,000 against capital employed of $1,250,000 gives 16.0% in 2024, and $300,000 against $1,500,000 gives 20.0% in 2025.

Evaluation: All three measures moved upward. The gross margin improved from 45.0% to 50.0%, consistent with better control of the 9,800 workbook waste rate and a mix shift toward higher-value recorded lessons. The operating margin rose from 12.5% to 15.0%, showing the $270,000 fixed costs were covered more efficiently as revenue grew from $1,600,000 to $2,000,000. The return on capital employed climbed from 16.0% to 20.0%, so the extra $250,000 of capital is working harder and supports the case for the $360,000 studio. Interest payable rose only from $20,000 to $25,000, so higher finance charges are not masking the improvement. Caution is needed: the 10% tutor absenteeism and 45 workbook complaints could erode these gains, and the better returns are measured against a 2024 base before the studio spend, so the new investment must earn at least the 20.0% now achieved.

Conclusion: MLC's profitability has improved — gross margin, operating margin and return on capital all rose together. The priority is to protect the 50.0% gross margin against 8.6% paper-cost inflation and to fill enough places for the $360,000 studio to maintain that return.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation and a justified conclusion on whether profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MLC of expanding its recorded lessons for the 61% of parents willing to pay $12 more.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 800 parents shows 61% would pay $12 more for recorded lessons and 72% want weekend classes, so MLC can raise revenue per unit from the $65 selling price toward $77 without adding variable cost per unit beyond $20, improving the $45 contribution and helping cover the $360,000 studio. Recorded lessons also fit the 4.3-out-of-5 satisfaction rating and can be sold repeatedly.

Disadvantage: Producing good recordings needs the $580 e-learning production course for tutors and may divert staff already stretched by 10% absenteeism and 45 workbook complaints. If pupils cannot ask questions live, the 96% pass rate could slip, and parents may resist the $12 premium if they perceive recorded lessons as inferior to classroom tuition, leaving the studio underused. The 45 workbook complaints and 3% waste rate already show how quickly quality slips when staff are stretched by 10% absenteeism, so recording quality must be protected as carefully as classroom teaching.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MLC's survey, costs and quality.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.4%, the 4.8% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in printing and paper costs will affect MLC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.9% to 4.4%): The $200,000 share issue needs no loan interest, so if MLC has no variable-rate borrowing the direct cost is zero; even if the $160,000 retained profit had instead been borrowed, a 0.5 percentage-point rise would add only 0.005 × $160,000 = $800 a year, tiny against $270,000 fixed costs. Higher rates may reduce parents' willingness to spend on private tutoring, but the direct financial hit is small and can be avoided.

Minimum wage increase (4.8%, to $13.60 an hour): With a workforce of 30, this raises the wage bill for tutors and support staff and cannot be opted out of. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the honest test is productivity of 11,000 units ÷ 30 staff = 366.67 units per worker. With $45 contribution per unit, a wage rise is affordable only while attendance holds near that level, otherwise the 10% absenteeism makes each unit of tuition more expensive.

Printing and paper inflation (8.6%): The insert does not decompose the $20 variable cost, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole $20 rose 8.6%, that is 0.086 × $20 = $1.72 per unit, or about $18,920 a year at 11,000 units, cutting contribution from $45 toward $43.28. The 5.5% exam-board licence rise adds a further fixed-pressure, though 3.1% growth in tutoring spend and the survey's $12 premium offer partial recovery.

Conclusion: The 8.6% rise in printing and paper costs will have the greatest impact. It hits every one of the 11,000 units and directly erodes the $45 contribution that funds the $360,000 studio, and it compounds the 45 workbook complaints and 5.5% licence rise. The interest-rate change is small and avoidable; the wage rise is manageable while productivity stays near 366.67 units per worker.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to MLC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MLC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MLC with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the others.
